claims.text: The AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles are nearly equiatomic.
The AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles have a homogeneous single-phase or uniformly mixed structure at room temperature.
In situ aberration-corrected TEM heating can reveal dynamic atomic-scale structural transformations in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
The observed transformations would provide direct experimental evidence of a theoretically predicted thermodynamic stabilization mechanism.
A heating stage can be used to ramp temperature while the nanoparticles are imaged in real time by aberration-corrected TEM.
The proposed temperature range is from room temperature to 700–1000 °C.
Using vacuum or an inert atmosphere will avoid oxidation during heating.
Heating induces atomic diffusion and surface reconstruction in the nanoparticles.
Thermally induced diffusion and reconstruction may produce local ordering, defects, or phase transformations.
Thermal activation increases atomic mobility and causes lattice rearrangements.
The lattice rearrangements reflect the influence of multicomponent thermodynamics.
Atomic rearrangements and changes in defect density can be observed in real time by high-resolution TEM.
Increasing temperature will produce surface reconstructions, defect migration, or transient phase formation.
The room-temperature nanoparticles exhibit a homogeneous and stable atomic arrangement.
The observed thermal behavior will depend on nanoparticle size distribution, heating rate, and tested temperature range.
Electron-beam exposure and environmental conditions may affect the observed structural behavior.
The onset temperature and precise nature of the atomic rearrangements are uncertain.
If no discernible atomic-scale changes occur over the tested range, or all changes are attributable solely to the electron beam, the proposed thermally induced transformation hypothesis is falsified.
